title: Luke, again
tomorrow: a vine and its branches. what does a branch actually have to do?

cards: Every family has one: the one who left. Moved away angry, stopped calling, came back changed or never came back. Jesus tells a story about that one.
A younger son asks for his inheritance early, leaves, spends it all, and ends up feeding pigs, hungry enough to want their food. He heads home with a speech rehearsed.
And then, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and running to him fell upon his neck, and kissed him." The father runs.

teach.h: A SHEEP, A COIN, A SON.
teach.b: The question underneath is old: what happens when the lost come back? Luke answers with three stories in a row: a lost sheep, a lost coin, a lost son. Each one ends in a party.
In the third, the son gets out only part of his speech, I am not worthy to be called thy son, before his father is calling for the best robe, a ring and shoes.
Then the older brother, who never left, refuses to come in, and the father goes out to him too. The neighbor who says this in another voice is Islam.

The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said, in a hadith in Sahih Muslim, that God is more glad when a servant turns back to him than a traveler who lost his camel in the desert, with all his food and water, lay down to die, and woke to find it standing beside him.
Muslims call that turning tawba. Same joy, in their own words. And one honest difference.

Catholics hear Luke's father as God and bring their return to confession, where a priest speaks the absolution. In Islam, tawba is between a person and God, with no one in between. Two homes, each with a door left open.

how: Catholics hear the parable of the prodigal son at Mass in Lent and bring their own return to God in the sacrament of confession, where the priest prays the words of absolution.

the apostle who wrote to the Romans
the Gospel writer of the father who runs

games.q: the lost, found — tap the pairs.
p: comes home with a speech ready
runs while he's still far off
won't go in to the party
a hadith of God's joy at return

s: the father makes his son finish the apology first
he calls for the robe, ring and shoes before the speech is done.
Luke tells three 'lost' stories in a row
a sheep, a coin, a son, each ending in a party.
the older brother is left outside without a word
the father goes out to him too.

games.q: your friend's sister left home after a big fight and now asks to visit. your friend is still hurt and says she has to earn it first. what does the father in Luke do?
o: runs to meet her, then deals with the hurt at home.
waits at the door until she proves she's changed.
sends word that the door is closed for now.
games.why: the father runs while his son is still far off, and later goes out to the angry older brother too.

practice: Close your eyes and bring to mind someone who has drifted: from family, from friends, from faith, or from themselves. Don't write them a speech.
Just stand at the end of the road in your mind, watching for them, the way the father did.

wordCard.voice: Luke. The Gospel writer who gives us the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the father who runs.

orig.note: Greek, Luke 15:20: he was moved with compassion, the moment before the father runs.

carryVoice: Your line: the father runs. He doesn't wait for the speech to finish. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and running to him fell upon his neck, and kissed him.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 2747 (also Sahih al-Bukhari 6309): God's joy at a servant's repentance, like a traveler finding his lost camel
